snippet.title: LED replacement bulbs for cars are bad and you shouldn't use them.
snippet.description:
A note for a common argument in the comments: yes Walmart is selling "the wrong ones..." but that's the problem! Average folks who stop by the automotive section because they have a tail light out might see "LED" as an upgrade, and unless they've gone down the enthusiast rabbit holes you or I might have, they won't have a reason to suspect Walmart (or other retailers) would be selling a *downgrade* (let alone a not-street-legal downgrade) and might very well pop them into their car.

Exactly like the previous owner of the Cube did.

snippet.title: Watch Out for Wrong Tyres for Your Electric Car ⚠️
snippet.description:
You’ve spent thousands of euros on your electric car… But are your tyres secretly sabotaging your range - or wearing out faster than they should?
Here’s a shocker: only 44 percent of EV drivers actually know what kind of tyres their car really needs. And no - not every tyre that fits your wheel is truly fit for your car.

The truth is, compared to petrol cars, electric cars put very different demands on their tyres - but how much does that really matter? Do electric cars really need special tyres - or is that just clever marketing?

▬ Video content ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
00:00 - 00:54: Intro EV tyres
00:55 - 01:56: Do EVs need special tyres?
01:57 - 03:26: Finding the right EV tyres
03:27 - 04:28: Why EV tyres are different
04:29 - 05:55: Buying guide for EV tyres
05:56 - 06:16: Are EV tyres more expensive?
06:17 - 06:37: Outro

Do electric cars really need tyres designed just for them?
Well, technically - not always. Most modern tyres today are EV-ready - you’ll often see “EVc”, short for Electric Vehicle Compatible, or “EVr”, short for Electric Vehicle Ready, stamped on the side. This tells you they’re designed with electric cars in mind, using stronger materials and low-resistance compounds to cope with extra weight and torque.
But here’s the important part: it only works one way. You can safely fit EV tyres on a petrol or diesel car - but not every regular tyre will perform well on an electric car. Electric cars are heavier, they deliver instant torque, and they are much quieter - so tyres that aren’t built for these purposes can wear out faster, get noisier, or slightly reduce your range.
The good news? Brands like Michelin, Continental, and Goodyear already offer EV-compatible models that handle everything effortlessly - so there’s no need to stress, just choose the right type.

How to Find the Right Tyres for Your EV?
Finding the right tyres for your electric car is easier than it sounds - here are four ways to go about it:
Option 1: Check your car’s registration certificate. If the tyre size, load, and speed ratings match - they are safe to buy even if they are regular tyres. However, they will typically lack additional features like advanced noise reduction or reinforced sidewalls for higher efficiency. 
Option 2: Go for EV-ready tyres. They started out as regular combustion car models but have been upgraded for electric vehicles - stronger compounds, higher load ratings, and lower noise to handle extra weight and instant torque. They’re easy to find - popular examples include the Bridgestone Turanza T005 and Goodyear Eagle F1 Asymmetric 6.
Brands like Michelin make it super simple: just enter your car model and tyre size on their website and you’ll instantly get a perfect match. Couldn’t be easier.
Option 3: Choose purpose-built EV tyres. These are designed from scratch for electric cars - like the Hankook iON or Falken e.Ziex - offering quieter rides and a longer lifespan.
Option 4: Select manufacturer-approved tyres. Tesla, for example, provides a list of manufacturer-approved tyres marked with a distinctive “T” at the centre. For Tesla vehicles, these are typically Pirelli models. They’re guaranteed to fit, but they are also on the pricey side.
If you ask us - Option 2 gives you the best mix of performance, comfort and cost.

Why EV Tyres Are Different:
Tyres for electric cars have a tougher job than you might think. Electric cars are heavier, quieter, and they accelerate instantly. This means their tyres need to be:
Strong enough to handle the extra battery weight
Grippy enough for instant torque
Quiet enough for peaceful driving
And heat-resistant to avoid wear from extra load

There are four key things that really make a difference when it comes to EV tyres:
1. Rolling resistance
2. Noise rating
3. Load index
4. Reinforced sidewalls

Are tyres for electric cars more expensive?
Yes, but for a good reason. EV tyres are built stronger and quieter - and these features cost more to produce. But they’re absolutely worth it. They last longer, they reduce cabin noise, and they can stretch your range - which means you’ll save money in the long run.
